03 / FOLLOW THE SCIENCE

From a river reading
to a human scale.

Follow the research pipeline. Select a step to look inside.

RESEARCH PIPELINE / INPUTS

Start with the watershed.

Rainfall, weather and basin characteristics describe the conditions upstream. They are the inputs to a model of how much water reaches the river.

The current explorer starts with observed USGS flow. Weather and basin model inputs are a planned integration.
THE HEIGHT ABOVE THE RIVERCONCEPTUAL CROSS-SECTION

HAND asks: “How high is this place above the river it drains to?” A calibrated water height is still required to estimate depth.

TWO EVENTS / ONE RIVER

Historical peaks at USGS gauge 03456500.

04 / LOOK BEYOND THE WATER

A flood doesn’t hit
everyone equally.

Flood maps ask where the water goes.
We’re asking who is there when it arrives.

REAL BUILDING FOOTPRINTS / STUDY WINDOW
WHO WAS IN THE WATER?

Every footprint
has a context.

Connect buildings to Census block groups to understand a community’s resources. Connect calibrated depths to understand exposure. Both matter.

THE RESEARCH AMBITION

The map isn’t the end product.
The decision is.

01 / PRIORITIZE

Warn the right
people first.

Help identify the neighborhoods that may face water earliest and deepest.

02 / RECOVER

Make recovery
more equitable.

Understand where flood exposure overlaps with fewer financial resources.

03 / REBUILD

Put decisions
in context.

Make rebuilding and long-term resilience conversations easier to understand.

04 / COMMUNICATE

Make the risk
feel real.

Connect an abstract river reading to the places people recognize.

RESEARCH DEMONSTRATION

Flood extents are illustrative. Calibrated ~10 m depths are a research target. This is not an official warning system. Follow the National Weather Service and local emergency management for real-time warnings. HAND alone does not resolve every bridge, debris jam, hydraulic structure, or flash-flood process.
